headings.title: Introduction to Pregnancy Diagnosis
headings.content: Diagnosis of pregnancy is a fundamental clinical skill required of every nursing and midwifery student practicing in Nigeria. Early and accurate identification of pregnancy ensures that expectant mothers receive timely prenatal care, which significantly reduces maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality rates in line with national health goals. The process of diagnosing pregnancy relies on a systematic evaluation of a woman's menstrual history, physical changes, and diagnostic testing. When a woman presents to a healthcare facility, the nurse must conduct a thorough health history, inquiring about her last normal menstrual period (LNMP), previous obstetric history, and any associated symptoms. Clinical diagnosis involves recognizing distinct physiological and anatomical alterations that occur in the maternal body following conception. These changes are traditionally categorized into three groups: presumptive, probable, and positive signs. Understanding these classifications helps healthcare providers differentiate between true gestation and other conditions that mimic pregnancy, such as phantom pregnancy, uterine fibroids, or ovarian cysts. Furthermore, laboratory tests and modern diagnostic tools like ultrasound provide definitive confirmation. As future nurses in Nigeria, students must master these clinical indicators to provide confident, evidence-based assessments in both urban tertiary hospitals and rural primary health care centers.

headings.title: Classification of Signs and Symptoms of Pregnancy
headings.content: The classification of the signs and symptoms of pregnancy is an essential framework that guides clinical assessment and decision-making for nursing students. These manifestations are divided into three distinct categories based on their reliability and clinical significance: presumptive, probable, and positive signs. Presumptive signs are subjective changes experienced by the woman herself, such as amenorrhea, nausea, fatigue, and breast tenderness. While these symptoms strongly suggest pregnancy, they are not diagnostic because they can be caused by other physiological or psychological conditions, such as hormonal imbalances or stress. Probable signs are objective changes observed and documented by the healthcare examiner during a physical assessment. Examples include uterine enlargement, changes in cervical and vaginal color such as Chadwick's sign, and positive results from over-the-counter or clinical urine pregnancy tests. Although these objective findings are highly indicative of gestation, they are still not absolute proof because conditions like pelvic tumors or ascites can yield similar physical findings. Finally, positive signs are absolute, objective indicators that are completely diagnostic of pregnancy, leaving no room for doubt. These include the visualization of the fetus via ultrasound, detection of fetal heart tones, and the active palpation of fetal movements by an experienced examiner. Mastering this classification system enables nurses to perform systematic evaluations, avoid misdiagnoses, and guide patients accurately through their early antenatal visits.

headings.title: Presumptive Signs of Pregnancy
headings.content: Presumptive signs of pregnancy are subjective indicators that prompt a woman to suspect she might be pregnant. For student nurses, recognizing these signs is vital during initial patient interviews. The most common and reliable presumptive sign in women with previously regular menstrual cycles is amenorrhea, or the sudden cessation of menses. However, amenorrhea can also be triggered by emotional stress, severe weight loss, endocrine disorders, or chronic illness. Other notable presumptive signs include nausea and vomiting, commonly referred to as 'morning sickness,' which typically occurs due to elevated levels of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) and estrogens during the first trimester. Urinary frequency is another frequent complaint caused by the early enlargement and pressure of the uterus on the bladder. Fatigue and exhaustion are widely reported as the body redirects significant metabolic energy toward supporting the developing conceptus. Breast changes, including tenderness, tingling sensations, heightened sensitivity, and the noticeable darkening of the areolae, also frequently occur. Additionally, some women experience quickening—the subjective sensation of fetal movement—though this is unreliable on its own because it can be mistaken for intestinal gas or peristalsis. Because all presumptive signs can be caused by factors other than pregnancy, a nurse must never rely on them alone for a definitive diagnosis, but rather use them to guide further objective assessment.

headings.title: Probable Signs of Pregnancy
headings.content: Probable signs of pregnancy are objective manifestations discovered by a healthcare provider during physical examination or through preliminary diagnostic testing. These signs strongly point toward pregnancy but remain short of absolute certainty. One classic probable sign is Goodell's sign, which involves the softening of the cervix due to increased vascularity and edema. Similarly, Chadwick's sign refers to the characteristic bluish-purple coloration of the vaginal mucosa, cervix, and vulva resulting from heightened local vascular congestion. Hegar's sign is another vital clinical finding identified during bimanual examination, characterized by the remarkable softening and compressibility of the lower uterine segment. Braxton Hicks contractions—irregular, painless uterine contractions that can occur throughout pregnancy—are also classified as probable signs. Furthermore, abdominal enlargement as the uterus grows out of the pelvic cavity becomes noticeable during the second trimester. Clinical and over-the-counter urine pregnancy tests, which detect the presence of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), fall under probable signs because rare conditions like hydatidiform moles or certain tumors can also secrete hCG and yield false-positive results. By mastering these physical examination techniques, nursing students can accurately identify high-probability indicators of gestation and prepare patients for confirmatory testing.

headings.title: Positive Signs of Pregnancy
headings.content: Positive signs of pregnancy provide absolute, undeniable confirmation that a fetus is present, leaving no room for alternative medical interpretations. These signs are detected exclusively through advanced clinical and technological methods that evaluate direct fetal structures or physiological activity. The visualization of the conceptus via ultrasound scanning is one of the most definitive positive signs. Real-time ultrasound can display the gestational sac, fetal cardiac activity, and fetal anatomical structures as early as the first trimester. Auscultation of fetal heart tones (FHTs) is another classic positive sign; using a Doppler ultrasound device, a skilled clinician can hear the distinct, rapid heartbeat of the fetus, which ranges between 110 and 160 beats per minute and is clearly distinguishable from the maternal pulse. Fetal heart sounds can also be heard using a specialized Fetoscope around the 18th to 20th week of gestation. Additionally, the active palpation of fetal movements by a trained healthcare professional, typically possible during the second half of pregnancy, serves as a reliable positive sign. Finally, later in gestation, the direct visualization and radiographic or ultrasound identification of the fetal skeleton confirms pregnancy beyond doubt. For student nurses, recognizing and understanding these positive signs ensures that clinical assessments are conclusive and that mothers receive appropriate, definitive confirmation of their prenatal status.

headings.title: Laboratory and Diagnostic Tests for Pregnancy
headings.content: Laboratory and diagnostic tests provide scientific validation of pregnancy by measuring specific biological markers or directly imaging the developing fetus. The primary hormonal marker utilized in pregnancy testing is human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), a glycoprotein produced by the developing syncytiotrophoblast shortly after fertilization and implantation. Serum and urine pregnancy assays are designed to detect hCG. Qualitative urine tests provide a simple 'yes or no' result and are widely used in primary healthcare clinics across Nigeria for rapid screening. Quantitative serum hCG tests measure the exact concentration of the hormone in the blood, which is particularly useful for monitoring early embryonic development, dating gestations, and diagnosing ectopic pregnancies or trophoblastic diseases. Ultrasonography is the premier diagnostic imaging tool in obstetrics. Transvaginal ultrasound can identify an intrauterine gestational sac as early as 4 to 5 weeks of gestation, while transabdominal ultrasound visualizes the fetus and fetal heartbeat slightly later, around 6 to 7 weeks. Other auxiliary tests, such as complete blood counts to check for anemia—a major concern among pregnant women in sub-Saharan Africa—and blood grouping with Rhesus factor determination, are routinely performed during initial diagnostic workups. Student nurses must understand how to interpret these test results and counsel patients on their implications for maternal and fetal health.

headings.title: Estimation of Expected Date of Delivery (EDD)
headings.content: The estimation of the Expected Date of Delivery (EDD), also known as the estimated date of confinement (EDC), is a vital calculation performed by nurses and midwives during the first antenatal visit. An accurate EDD helps in monitoring fetal growth, planning appropriate timing for diagnostic screenings, and preparing the mother for labor and delivery. The most widely accepted clinical method for calculating EDD is Naegele's Rule. To apply Naegele's Rule, the healthcare provider takes the first day of the woman's Last Normal Menstrual Period (LNMP), adds seven days, adds one year, and then subtracts three months; alternatively, adding seven days to the LNMP and counting forward nine calendar months yields the same result. For example, if a woman's LNMP began on May 10th, adding 7 days gives May 17th, and subtracting 3 months places the EDD on February 17th of the following year. Naegele's Rule assumes a standard 28-day menstrual cycle with ovulation occurring on the 14th day; therefore, nurses must adjust the calculation if the woman has irregular cycles or a known history of prolonged or shortened follicular phases. In modern clinical practice, especially when the LNMP is uncertain or forgotten, early first-trimester obstetric ultrasound is considered the most accurate tool for dating pregnancy, as crown-rump length (CRL) measurements have a very small margin of error. Mastering both Naegele's Rule and ultrasound dating ensures that nursing students can accurately compute gestational age in diverse clinical settings.

headings.title: Nursing Role and Patient Counseling in Pregnancy Diagnosis
headings.content: The nursing role in pregnancy diagnosis extends far beyond clinical assessment and laboratory testing; it encompasses compassionate communication, emotional support, and comprehensive patient counseling. When a woman visits a healthcare facility for pregnancy confirmation, she may experience a wide spectrum of emotions—ranging from profound joy and relief to anxiety, fear, or distress, particularly if the pregnancy is unintended or complicated by socioeconomic challenges. The nurse must maintain a non-judgmental, empathetic attitude, creating a safe and confidential environment where the patient feels comfortable discussing her reproductive health. Counseling sessions should cover the interpretation of test results, the importance of early and regular antenatal care (ANC), nutritional education, avoidance of teratogens (such as alcohol, tobacco, and harmful self-medication), and the identification of danger signs during pregnancy. In the Nigerian context, nurses also play a vital role in addressing cultural myths and misconceptions surrounding pregnancy diagnosis and maternal health. Furthermore, nurses provide guidance on maternal nutrition, emphasizing locally available, nutrient-dense foods, and prescribe essential supplements like routine iron and folic acid. By combining clinical competency with empathetic counseling, nursing students prepare themselves to become pillars of maternal and child health support in their communities.
